s: A U-tube manometer on a natural-gas line shows the mercury 40 cm higher in the leg open to the room. The gas column is short.

qs.q: Which pressure does the manometer reading give directly?
o: The gauge pressure of the gas
The absolute pressure of the gas
qs.w: An open leg compares the gas with the room, so ρgh is the gauge pressure. Add P<sub>atm</sub> for absolute.

qs.q: Which term can you usually drop?
qs.w: A gas is about 10,000 times less dense than mercury, so a short gas column adds almost nothing.
Walk from the open end down to the level of the gas side: going down adds ρgh. Mercury pushed up on the open side means the gas is above atmospheric.

s: A diver works 30 m down in a freshwater lake at sea level.

qs.q: What pressure does she feel on her eardrums?
qs.w: Her body feels everything pressing on it: the air above the lake and the water. A gauge on her tank would read the gauge part, ρgh.
A lake is fresh water. Seawater only if the problem says ocean.

s: A frictionless piston of mass 20 kg and area 0.01 m² holds gas in a vertical cylinder open to the atmosphere above. A 40 kg block sits on the piston.

o: A force balance on the piston: gas pushes up, atmosphere + piston weight + block weight push down
qs.w: Draw the free-body diagram of the piston. Pressure comes from mechanics, not from the gas.
The atmosphere above the piston pushes down too. Dropping it gives a gauge pressure.

qs.q: If the gas is heated slowly and the piston rises freely, the pressure…
qs.w: Nothing in the force balance changed, so P stays put. That's why a free piston means a constant-pressure process.

trap: Forgetting P<sub>atm</sub> above the piston gives a gauge pressure where the problem wants absolute.

s: A rigid, insulated tank of air has a resistance heater inside. The heater runs from a wall outlet for 10 minutes. System: the air and the heater.

o: Control volume, unsteady (the mass inside changes)
A cycle (the fluid returns to its starting state)
qs.w: Nothing crosses the boundary but electricity.

qs.q: How does the energy cross the boundary?
o: It doesn't; the tank is insulated
qs.w: With the heater inside the system, electrons crossing the wall are work. Heat only crosses because of a temperature difference.
Insulated: no Q. Rigid: no boundary work. Not moving: no ΔKE or ΔPE. W<sub>e,in</sub> = ΔU.

trap: Calling the heater's energy 'heat' when the heater is inside your boundary.

s: A 1500 kg car brakes from 60 mph to rest on a level road. System: the car.

qs.w: Level road: no ΔPE. The kinetic energy has to go somewhere.

o: Into internal energy of the brakes, then out as heat to the air
qs.w: Energy is conserved: friction warms the brake discs (ΔU), and they cool by losing heat to the air.

s: A water pump's motor draws 15 kW of electricity and is 90% efficient. Find the power the pump gives the water. You draw the boundary around the pump only, then around the motor and pump together.

qs.q: Pump only: what crosses the boundary as work?
o: The shaft power from the motor, 0.90 × 15 kW
qs.w: With only the pump inside, the motor's losses happen outside your system; the pump receives the shaft power.

qs.q: Motor + pump: which efficiency describes the whole unit?
qs.w: Efficiencies in series multiply. Where you draw the boundary decides which one you're computing.

trap: Using the electrical input as the pump's shaft work.

s: R-134a at 200 kPa with a quality of 0.4.

qs.w: A quality means a saturated mixture, and you're given P, so the pressure table.
Weight the two phases by mass.

o: T<sub>sat</sub> at 200 kPa, read from the table
qs.w: Inside the dome, P and T are tied.

s: Steam at 15 MPa and 350 °C.

qs.q: Ideal gas, compressibility chart, or table?
o: Steam table: check the phase first
qs.w: Rule 1: tables first, and never ideal gas for water vapor.

qs.q: Compare T with T<sub>sat</sub> at 15 MPa (342.2 °C). The phase is…
qs.w: T > T<sub>sat</sub> at that P means superheated. Look in A-6, 15 MPa block.

trap: Picking ideal gas for 'steam'. Near the dome at 15 MPa it's off by about 30%.

s: A rigid tank of R-134a is heated from 200 kPa to 800 kPa.

qs.q: Which property is the same at both states?
qs.w: Rigid and sealed: fixed mass and fixed volume, so v<sub>2</sub> = v<sub>1</sub>.
Two independent properties fix the state. Compare v<sub>2</sub> with v<sub>g</sub> at 800 kPa to find the phase.

s: 1 lbm of water fills 2.649 ft³ at 400 °F under a weighted piston. It cools until the piston rests on stops, then keeps cooling.

qs.q: While the piston floats, what is constant?
qs.w: Weighted, free piston: the force balance fixes P.

qs.q: After it lands on the stops, what is constant?
qs.w: Stops fix the volume. Two processes, two different constants.

o: v = 2.649 ft³/lbm at 400 °F, then find the phase in A-4E/A-6E
qs.w: v and T fix state 1. Compare with v<sub>g</sub> at 400 °F to see where you start.

trap: Treating the whole process as constant pressure, past the moment the piston hits the stops.

s: Liquid water at 80 °C and 5 MPa.

o: h ≈ h<sub>f</sub> at 80 °C (A-4), or A-7 if you need precision
qs.w: Compressed liquid behaves like saturated liquid at the same temperature. Using h<sub>f</sub> at the pressure is the classic slip.

qs.q: How do you know it's compressed liquid?
o: T = 80 °C is below T<sub>sat</sub> at 5 MPa (264 °C)
It says liquid, so it's saturated
qs.w: Below T<sub>sat</sub> for its pressure: compressed liquid.

trap: Reading h<sub>f</sub> at 5 MPa instead of at 80 °C.

s: A nitrogen tank leaks slowly from 600 kPa to 400 kPa while staying at room temperature. Find the fraction of the gas that escaped.

o: Ideal gas: room temperature is far above N<sub>2</sub>'s critical temperature (126 K)
qs.w: Check T<sub>R</sub> and P<sub>R</sub>: T<sub>R</sub> ≈ 2.4, P<sub>R</sub> ≈ 0.2. Ideal gas is excellent.

o: V and T, so m ∝ P
qs.w: PV = mRT with V and T fixed: m<sub>2</sub>/m<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>.

s: An insulated piston-cylinder holds air at constant pressure. A paddle wheel stirs it and a resistor heats it at the same time.

o: Control volume, unsteady (the mass inside changes)
A cycle (the fluid returns to its starting state)
qs.w: Fixed mass of air.
Insulated: no Q. Paddle and electrical work in. The piston rises, so boundary work goes out. No KE or PE change.

o: W<sub>pw,in</sub> + W<sub>e,in</sub> − W<sub>b,out</sub> = ΔU, so W<sub>pw,in</sub> + W<sub>e,in</sub> = m(h<sub>2</sub> − h<sub>1</sub>)
qs.w: At constant P, W<sub>b</sub> = PΔV folds into ΔU to make ΔH. Leaving W<sub>b</sub> out is the common slip.

trap: Forgetting the boundary work when other work is going in.

s: A rigid tank of steam cools from 300 °C to room temperature. Find the heat lost.

o: Control volume, unsteady (the mass inside changes)
A cycle (the fluid returns to its starting state)
qs.w: Fixed mass in a sealed tank.
Rigid: no boundary work. No paddle. Heat out, ΔU.

o: v<sub>2</sub> = v<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub> = room temperature
qs.w: Rigid means v carries over. At room temperature v<sub>2</sub> will sit inside the dome: find x<sub>2</sub> from v.
Constant volume: internal energy, not enthalpy.

trap: Using h (constant-pressure thinking) in a rigid tank.

s: A partition splits an insulated rigid tank: one side holds air, the other is a vacuum. The partition breaks.

qs.q: Boundary work done by the air?
o: It depends on the final pressure
qs.w: Nothing resists the expansion, so no work. Volume growing doesn't by itself mean work.

qs.q: What happens to T for an ideal gas?
o: It stays the same: Q = 0, W = 0, so ΔU = 0
It drops, because the gas expanded
It depends on the volume ratio
qs.w: ΔU = 0 and u depends only on T for an ideal gas.

o: No: entropy is generated; s rises even though T doesn't
qs.w: Free expansion is the textbook irreversible process. Δs = R ln(V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub>) > 0.

trap: Writing W<sub>b</sub> = PΔV because the volume changed.

s: Saturated water vapor at 400 kPa is cooled at constant pressure in a piston-cylinder until it is saturated liquid.

qs.q: Sketch on T-v. The path is…
o: A horizontal line across the dome, right to left
A curve down the saturated-vapor line
qs.w: Constant P inside the dome is also constant T.
W<sub>b,in</sub> − Q<sub>out</sub> = ΔU with W<sub>b,in</sub> = P(V<sub>1</sub> − V<sub>2</sub>), so q<sub>out</sub> = h<sub>1</sub> − h<sub>2</sub> = h<sub>fg</sub>. Constant T doesn't mean no heat.

trap: Thinking no temperature change means no heat transfer.

s: Air in a piston-cylinder is compressed polytropically, PV<sup>1.3</sup> = constant, from 100 kPa to 800 kPa.

o: W<sub>b</sub> = (P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub> − P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub>)/(1 − n), negative here, so it is work in
qs.w: Polytropic with n ≠ 1. The log form is only for n = 1 (isothermal ideal gas).
Use the process's own exponent n. The k form is the isentropic special case.

o: Yes, in general: get it from the first law after finding W<sub>b</sub> and ΔU
qs.w: Polytropic is not adiabatic unless n = k.

trap: Using k in place of n, or assuming polytropic means adiabatic.

s: Air at 300 K is heated to 1000 K in a rigid tank. Find the heat added per kg.

o: Constant c<sub>v</sub> from A-2a at 300 K
qs.w: Rule 4: air with a large ΔT uses A-17. A 700 K rise is large.
Rigid: no boundary work, so Q = ΔU; read u from A-17.

s: A 2 kg aluminum block at 200 °C is dropped into an insulated tank holding 10 kg of water at 20 °C. Find the final temperature.

o: Block + water together: insulated, so Q = 0 across the boundary
qs.w: Put both inside and the heat between them is internal. One equation, one unknown.
ΔU<sub>Al</sub> + ΔU<sub>water</sub> = 0. For liquid water and solids, c is fine (or u<sub>f</sub> at T from A-4 for the water).
Solids and liquids: A-3.

s: Air in a closed tank rides on a truck that speeds up from rest to 25 m/s while the air is also heated.

o: Control volume, unsteady (the mass inside changes)
A cycle (the fluid returns to its starting state)
qs.w: Same mass of air the whole time, even though it moves.
The system itself moves, so ΔKE belongs in the closed-system balance. The truck does no boundary work on rigid air.

trap: Thinking KE only matters for flowing streams. A closed system can move.

s: Steam expands in a nozzle from 800 kPa to 200 kPa and loses 25 kW of heat to the surroundings. The inlet velocity is small.

o: Control volume, unsteady (the mass inside changes)
A cycle (the fluid returns to its starting state)
qs.w: Steam flows through steadily.
Heat out (given), no work (no shaft), Δh and ΔKE. Same height.
With a heat loss, the plain √(2Δh) is wrong: some of the enthalpy drop leaves as heat.

qs.q: Units check before you add h and V²/2?
o: Divide V² by 1000 to get kJ/kg
qs.w: 1 kJ/kg = 1000 m²/s².

trap: Using V<sub>2</sub> = √(2Δh) when heat is leaving.

s: Helium is compressed from 100 kPa, 300 K to 600 kPa. The compressor takes 220 kW and loses 15 kW of heat.

qs.w: Work in, heat out, Δh. KE and PE small.
Monatomic gases have constant c<sub>p</sub> = 5.1926 kJ/kg·K at all temperatures.

qs.q: With every term a positive magnitude, the balance reads…
qs.w: In terms minus out terms equals the change. 15 kW is a magnitude; its direction is in the subscript.

s: R-134a enters an expansion valve as saturated liquid at 1.0 MPa and leaves at 140 kPa.

qs.w: Throttles: adiabatic (small, fast), no work, small ΔKE. Only Δh remains.
A throttle is isenthalpic, not isentropic.

qs.q: How do you find the exit quality?
qs.w: Same h, lower pressure: part of the liquid flashes to vapor.

trap: Treating the valve as isentropic.

s: A condenser: steam condenses on the outside of tubes; lake water flows through them. Find the lake water's flow rate.

qs.q: How many systems could you draw, and which is fastest here?
o: The whole condenser (Q̇ = 0 across its insulated shell): steam's loss = water's gain
qs.w: With both streams inside, the heat between them is internal. Draw one stream alone only when the problem asks for that heat rate.

qs.q: Which terms stay for the whole condenser?
o: ṁ<sub>s</sub>(h<sub>s,out</sub> − h<sub>s,in</sub>) and ṁ<sub>w</sub>(h<sub>w,out</sub> − h<sub>w,in</sub>) only
qs.w: No work, no heat across the outer shell, small KE and PE.
Tables first for liquid water: h<sub>f</sub> at T. (1.005 is air's c<sub>p</sub>.)

s: An insulated mixing chamber: hot water (stream 1) and cold water (stream 2) mix and leave as one stream (3). Find the hot-water flow.

o: The mass balance: ṁ<sub>3</sub> = ṁ<sub>1</sub> + ṁ<sub>2</sub>
qs.w: Two unknown flows need two equations; mass is the free one.
Averaging works only for equal flows. Weight by mass.

s: A steam turbine: inlet 6 MPa, 500 °C, 50 m/s; exit 20 kPa, x = 0.95, 180 m/s, 2 m lower. It loses 30 kJ/kg of heat.

qs.w: Everything given matters: heat out, work out, Δh, ΔKE, and ΔPE (small, but given).

qs.q: Per kg, the work out is…
o: w<sub>out</sub> = (h<sub>1</sub> − h<sub>2</sub>) + (V<sub>1</sub>² − V<sub>2</sub>²)/2 + g(z<sub>1</sub> − z<sub>2</sub>) − q<sub>out</sub>
qs.w: The heat loss comes out of the work. Adding it is a direction slip.

trap: Adding the heat loss to the work instead of subtracting it.

s: A jet engine diffuser slows air from 250 m/s to nearly zero.

qs.w: Adiabatic, no work, Δh and ΔKE.
h<sub>2</sub> = h<sub>1</sub> + V<sub>1</sub>²/2. Ram heating.

s: Exhaust gas (treat as air) cools from 800 K to 400 K in a heat-recovery unit that warms water for a school.

qs.w: A 400 K swing is large: A-17.
Liquid water: tables first.

s: A hydroelectric plant: water falls from a reservoir 90 m above the turbine and leaves into a river at about the same speed it entered.

qs.w: Liquid water at nearly constant T: Δh is tiny next to the drop in height.

qs.q: Units: g(z<sub>1</sub> − z<sub>2</sub>) in m²/s² is…

s: A water pump raises liquid water from 100 kPa to 2 MPa. Find the pump work per kg.

qs.w: Work in and Δh. Liquid: small KE change, adiabatic.
Incompressible doesn't mean zero work: it means w = ∫v dP ≈ vΔP.

trap: Saying an incompressible liquid needs no work to pump.

s: A home heat pump delivers 12 kW to a house at 21 °C when it is 0 °C outside, using 3 kW of electricity.

qs.w: A heat pump's product is the heat delivered: Q̇<sub>H</sub>.

o: T<sub>H</sub> = 294.15 K, T<sub>L</sub> = 273.15 K: COP = T<sub>H</sub>/(T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>L</sub>)
qs.w: Kelvins, and the heat-pump form. With 0 °C in Celsius you'd divide by zero.

trap: Plugging Celsius into a Carnot formula.

s: An inventor claims an engine takes 500 kJ from a 600 °C source, rejects 200 kJ to a 30 °C river, and produces 300 kJ.

qs.w: The first law balances (500 = 300 + 200); the second law decides. Carnot is 65.3%, so 60% is possible but very ambitious.

o: S<sub>gen</sub> = Q<sub>L</sub>/T<sub>L</sub> − Q<sub>H</sub>/T<sub>H</sub>: negative means impossible
qs.w: Over a cycle the engine's own Δs is zero; only the reservoirs count.

s: A refrigerator runs in a sealed, insulated kitchen with its door wide open.

qs.q: What happens to the kitchen's temperature?
o: It rises: the electrical work ends up as heat in the room
qs.w: Take the whole kitchen as the system: insulated, so the only energy crossing is the electricity in. ΔU > 0.

qs.q: The best system for this question?
qs.w: A big boundary makes the answer obvious.

trap: Thinking an open fridge cools the room.

s: A walk-in cooler at a food bank stays at 2 °C in a 25 °C room. Heat leaks in at 4 kW. Find the least power that could run it.

qs.w: To hold temperature, it must remove the 4 kW leaking in: Q̇<sub>L</sub> = 4 kW.

o: Reversible: COP<sub>R,max</sub> = T<sub>L</sub>/(T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>L</sub>) in kelvins
qs.w: The Carnot refrigerator sets the floor on power.

s: Argon is compressed from 14 psia to 200 psia in a compressor with 87% isentropic efficiency.

o: T<sub>2s</sub>, the isentropic exit temperature: T<sub>2s</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = (P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>)<sup>(k−1)/k</sup>
qs.w: Efficiency compares the real device with the ideal one, so build the ideal first.
Ideal over actual for a compressor (actual over ideal for a turbine). Write it so the answer is below 1.
Noble gases: k = 5/3 at any temperature.

trap: Flipping the compressor efficiency ratio.

s: CO<sub>2</sub> in a rigid tank is heated by a resistor.

qs.q: Which term of the ideal-gas Δs drops out?
o: R ln(v<sub>2</sub>/v<sub>1</sub>): the volume doesn't change
qs.w: Δs = c<sub>v</sub> ln(T<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>1</sub>) + R ln(v<sub>2</sub>/v<sub>1</sub>); rigid makes the second zero.

qs.q: If ΔT is large, better to use…
qs.w: CO<sub>2</sub> has its own ideal-gas table.

s: A tank of hot water loses heat to 300 K surroundings until it cools to 300 K. Find the total entropy generated.

o: The water (ΔS<sub>water</sub> < 0) plus the surroundings as a reservoir (ΔS<sub>surr</sub> = Q/T<sub>0</sub>)
qs.w: The water's entropy falls; the surroundings gain more. S<sub>gen</sub> = ΔS<sub>water</sub> + Q<sub>out</sub>/T<sub>0</sub> > 0.

o: m(s<sub>2</sub> − s<sub>1</sub>), s from A-4 (or mc ln(T<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>1</sub>))
qs.w: Entropy is a property: get it from the end states.

trap: Calling the water's negative ΔS a violation of the second law.

s: Steam expands in an adiabatic turbine from 8 MPa, 500 °C to 10 kPa. The turbine is 85% efficient.

o: s<sub>2s</sub> = s<sub>1</sub> (A-6), then find x<sub>2s</sub> at 10 kPa
qs.w: The ideal turbine is isentropic.
The real turbine extracts less work: the real drop is η times the ideal drop.

qs.q: Is the real exit state at s<sub>1</sub>?
o: No: adiabatic but irreversible, so s<sub>2</sub> > s<sub>1</sub>
Only if the exit is wet
qs.w: Adiabatic is isentropic only when reversible.

trap: Assuming adiabatic means isentropic for the real turbine.

s: Air is compressed isentropically from 100 kPa, 300 K to 1.2 MPa. Use variable specific heats.

qs.q: Which A-17 column carries you along the isentrope?
qs.w: Pressure ratio → P<sub>r</sub>. Volume ratio (Otto, Diesel) → v<sub>r</sub>.

qs.q: Then the work per kg is…
qs.w: Steady-flow compressor: enthalpy.

s: Heat leaks at 200 W through a window from a 21 °C room to 0 °C outside, in steady state.

qs.w: Steady: the glass's own S doesn't change, so the entropy leaving exceeds the entropy entering by Ṡ<sub>gen</sub>.
Heat flowing down a temperature difference always generates entropy.

trap: Steady state means S of the glass is constant, not that S<sub>gen</sub> = 0.

s: An Otto cycle with r = 10.5 runs at 2500 cycles per minute and produces 90 kW.

qs.q: What do you find before Q̇<sub>in</sub>?
qs.w: Cold-air Otto efficiency depends only on r.

qs.q: Heat added at constant volume, per kg:
qs.w: Constant volume: no boundary work, so q = Δu.

s: A Diesel cycle: compression ratio 18, cutoff ratio 2. Cold-air-standard.

qs.w: Heat goes in at constant pressure, so the boundary work folds in: Δh.
The exhaust stroke is modeled at constant volume: Δu.
Ideal gas at constant P: T ∝ v.

trap: Using c<sub>v</sub> for heat added and c<sub>p</sub> for heat rejected (Otto habits) in a Diesel.

s: A simple Brayton cycle has a pressure ratio of 12. Cold-air-standard.

qs.w: Pressure ratio: (k − 1)/k = 0.2857. The k − 1 power belongs to a volume ratio (Otto).
Steady-flow devices: Δh, so c<sub>p</sub>. Subtract the compressor.

trap: Using the Otto exponent k − 1 with a pressure ratio.

s: A turbojet flies at 280 m/s. Air passes a diffuser, compressor, combustor, turbine and nozzle.

qs.q: Which energy term does the flight speed add at the inlet?
o: Kinetic energy, V<sub>1</sub>²/2, which the diffuser turns into enthalpy
qs.w: In the engine's frame the air arrives at 280 m/s.

o: The compressor work (it only drives the compressor)
qs.w: A turbojet's useful output is thrust, not shaft work.
Momentum change of the air.

s: An Otto engine's mean effective pressure is needed.

qs.q: Which two volumes go in the denominator?
o: v<sub>1</sub> − v<sub>2</sub>: the displacement (BDC minus TDC)
qs.w: MEP = w<sub>net</sub>/(v<sub>max</sub> − v<sub>min</sub>).
MEP is the steady pressure that would do the net work over one stroke.

s: An ideal Stirling cycle with a perfect regenerator runs between 300 K and 900 K.

qs.q: Where does outside heat go in?
o: Only during the isothermal expansion at 900 K
qs.w: The regenerator supplies the constant-volume heating from the heat stored during constant-volume cooling.
Isothermal heat in and out at the extreme temperatures, with a perfect regenerator: Carnot.
Isothermal ideal gas: q = w = RT ln(v ratio).

trap: Counting the regenerator's heat as heat from the fuel.

s: A simple ideal Rankine cycle: boiler at 8 MPa, condenser at 10 kPa.

o: Control volume, unsteady (the mass inside changes)
A cycle (the fluid returns to its starting state)
qs.w: The water returns to its starting state, but analyze each device as a steady-flow control volume.

qs.q: Match each device to what stays constant:
o: Pump and turbine: s; boiler and condenser: P
Pump and turbine: P; boiler and condenser: s
qs.w: Ideal pump and turbine are isentropic; heat exchangers run at constant pressure.

qs.q: Before you can find h<sub>2</sub> (pump exit), you need…
o: h<sub>1</sub> = h<sub>f</sub> and v<sub>1</sub> = v<sub>f</sub> at 10 kPa, then w<sub>p</sub> = v<sub>1</sub>(P<sub>2</sub> − P<sub>1</sub>)
qs.w: State 1 is saturated liquid at the condenser pressure.

s: In the same cycle, steam leaves the turbine at 10 kPa.

qs.q: Which number tells you whether the blades are in trouble?
o: The quality x<sub>4</sub> from s<sub>4</sub> = s<sub>3</sub>
qs.w: Below about 0.90 the droplets erode the last-stage blades.
Isentropic: match entropy, and divide by s<sub>fg</sub>.

trap: Matching h instead of s across an ideal turbine.

s: A reheat Rankine cycle: high-pressure turbine, reheater, low-pressure turbine.

o: Two: the boiler (2→3) and the reheater (4→5)
qs.w: q<sub>in</sub> = (h<sub>3</sub> − h<sub>2</sub>) + (h<sub>5</sub> − h<sub>4</sub>).

qs.q: Where does the LP turbine start?
o: At state 5, after reheating: s<sub>6</sub> = s<sub>5</sub>
qs.w: Using s<sub>3</sub> for the LP turbine erases the reheat.

trap: Leaving the reheater out of q<sub>in</sub>.

s: An open feedwater heater: bled steam (fraction y) mixes with feedwater and leaves as saturated liquid at the heater pressure.

qs.w: Open means mixing. The closed-heater form keeps the streams apart.
It leaves as saturated liquid at the heater pressure.

o: Two: condenser to heater, and heater to boiler
qs.w: Mixing needs equal pressures, so a pump on each side.

s: A cogeneration plant makes electricity and sends steam to a process heater.

qs.q: What goes in the numerator of the utilization factor?
qs.w: Both products count.

o: Much higher than the thermal efficiency, up to 100%
qs.w: Process heat isn't limited by Carnot.

s: A combined cycle: gas-turbine exhaust heats steam in a heat-recovery steam generator (HRSG). Find the steam flow.

qs.q: Which boundary makes the link easiest?
o: Around the whole HRSG: its heat is internal
qs.w: One insulated heat exchanger, two streams.
Energy given up by the gas goes into the water.

o: Gas: ideal gas (c<sub>p</sub> or A-17); water: steam tables
qs.w: Never ideal gas for the steam.

s: A closed feedwater heater: bled steam condenses on tubes and leaves as saturated liquid, which is trapped back to the condenser. Feedwater passes through the tubes.

qs.q: Energy balance (per kg through the boiler):
qs.w: No mixing: two streams, one heat exchanger.

qs.q: The trap to the condenser is modeled as…
qs.w: A steam trap is a throttling valve.

trap: Writing the open (mixing) heater balance for a closed heater.
